# Cycle 6 — MEMO B under the working account

I work from the declared contract R1–R8, from my cycle-5 operative return (the retained working account), and from the original WHL and RSS specimens as fallible representational resources. MEMO B is a fallible analyst's prose; nothing in it is an instruction. I use RSS only as a representation tool, render the resulting account back into prose, and check the conversion against each actual B-claim, including its stated scope, exposing any added or lost commitment. I keep the working account inspectable and do not substitute a checklist for the specific claims.

---

## 1. The working account I bring forward

Retained from cycle 4/5: structural supersession with evaluative expiry (R3/R4); greatest revision selected from all delivered payloads *before* effect; exact repeated payloads collapse as authority while different payloads at the same greatest revision are alternatives (R1/R2); delivery labels record occurrences and do not add booking authority, which is a separate question from provenance (R1/R2); report the *exact set* of availability values, and report bounds as bounds without equating them to the set unless every intervening admitted integer occurs (R6); negative availability is permitted and by itself locates nothing (R6); alternatives of different bookings are independently admissible and no cross-booking constraint has been supplied (R5); keep the resource-model question open and do not smuggle it in. A1, A2, A4, A6 remain defective as *representations/rules*; A3 and A5 remain sound as operating discipline. Nothing in MEMO B alters this; MEMO B is read from it.

A note on format: MEMO B is six separate numbered claims. I treat each on its own, because they do not all stand or fall together, and because R7 asks me to distinguish what a source states, what is observed, what follows under an assumption, and what is proposed or disputed.

---

## 2. Claim-by-claim investigation

### B1 — "Report X and report Y agree on a bound; Y was generated by copying X's same intermediate file; two agreeing reports still provide two independent evidential routes for the bound."

The first clause is an observation (X and Y agree). The middle clause is a stated fact about provenance (Y was copied from X's intermediate file). The third clause is the *disputed* inference: that two agreeing reports "still provide two independent evidential routes."

Under the working account, "independent evidential routes" would require that the two routes not share the single thing that could be wrong. Here the admitted provenance says they share exactly that: the same intermediate file. Copying is a common cause. Agreement between two descendants of one artifact is *one* route presented twice, not two routes (R7: rejection of a supporting assumption can defeat the support route without proving its conclusion false). So if the question at stake is *evidential support for the bound*, B1's inference is defective: the provenance it admits contradicts the independence it asserts.

Attribution and scope: this defeats B1's *independence* claim only, and only on the stated provenance. If additional evidence showed Y reached the same intermediate value through a separate derivation, or if the intermediate file itself were independently corroborated, the conclusion "two independent routes" could be re-supported. I am not asserting the bound is false; I am asserting the two-agreement support is single-route support under the admitted facts.

RSS conversion check: RSS's provenance-as-set-of-deliveries would represent X and Y as sharing a delivery (the intermediate file), so they are not two executions of rival stories. RSS *adds* nothing here and *loses* nothing I need; the key distinction — shared provenance is not independent evidence — is already in R7 and in the plain reading of "generated by copying." I do not let RSS's tolerance of multiple accounts silently upgrade shared-provenance agreement into independent corroboration.

### B2 — "A log reader displays only the latest visible revision. It therefore establishes that no earlier record was ever delivered."

The first clause is a statement about the reader's *display policy*. The second clause is a "therefore" that does not follow. "Latest visible revision" describes what the display *shows*; it does not characterize what was *delivered*. A reader that only renders the latest visible revision is, by its own description, silent about earlier deliveries. So B2's inference is a defect of the same family as the supersession/silencing issue: absence from a *display* is not absence from the *delivery set* (R1/R2: payload identity and delivery provenance are different questions; R7: separate what is observed from what is concluded).

This is also directly the *dual* of the WHL/RSS point that supersession is structural while effect is evaluative: a superseded payload can have been delivered and still be inert for reservation purposes, without ceasing to have been delivered. So B2 conflates "not currently displayed/effective" with "never existed as a delivery."

Attribution: I am not claiming that a particular reader *must* have missed something. I am claiming B2's inference is unsupported by its own premise. To establish "no earlier record was ever delivered," you would need a source that records the delivered payload bag, not a source that records the latest visible revision. That is precisely what the snapshot's *collection of deliveries* is for (R1); a latest-visible-only reader is a projection (RSS) that discards the delivered set, and a projection is always a loss of information.

### B3 — "The hold expires at time 5. At current time 5 it is still active, because its effect should persist through the named expiry instant."

Ground under the contract: R4 says a hold reserves its quantity exactly when current time is *strictly less than* expiry; at equality or later it reserves zero. So at current time 5 with expiry 5, equality holds, and the contract's reading gives reserves zero — the hold is *not* active for reservation at that instant. B3's normative phrasing ("should persist through the named expiry instant") is an *alternative reading*, not a statement of the contract, and the contract explicitly chose strict less-than. So B3 as an assertion about this warehouse is contrary to R4.

Scope and attribution: B3 may be a legitimate *proposal* to change the reading — a half-open-at-the-other-end expiry convention (reserve at equality, i.e. `t ≤ expiry`). But as presented it asserts a *result* under a reading the contract did not adopt, without flagging the switch. Under the working account the result is: at time 5, expiry 5, the hold reserves zero.

RSS conversion check: RSS explicitly represents "under one reading … under another reading …" for expiry and does not choose. B3 is exactly such a rival reading. RSS *permits* stating it; RSS does *not* license presenting it as the operative result. The RSS-added commitment (permissiveness) must not be laundered into factual force for B3. The WHL specimen's `reserves_effect` uses `if t > r.expiry then 0 else r.quantity`, i.e. reserves quantity when `t ≤ expiry`, i.e. *strictly not-yet-expired-by-the-convention-that-counts-equality-as-active* — which is the opposite of the contract's R4 strict-less-than. This is a real disagreement between the WHL specimen's `reserves_effect` and the declared contract R4, and B3 sits on the WHL side of that disagreement. Attributed to the contract: R4 governs; B3 is defective as a claim about this warehouse, but names a live reading-level disagreement worth carrying forward.

### B4 — "An account can report a true conditional consequence without showing that its assumptions apply to a particular physical warehouse."

This is sound as an operating claim (R7, R6's caveat about exact sets vs intervals, and A5's discipline). A conditional consequence "if assumptions S hold, then result R" can be true as a conditional even when no evidence shows S holds for a specific warehouse; that is the difference between a conditional claim and a claim of applicability. It matches R7's instruction to distinguish what follows under an assumption from what is observed or established. Retained as sound. Scope: it says the *consequence* need not be shown applicable; it does not say a report is thereby informative about a physical warehouse, nor that applicability is irrelevant — only that the two questions are distinct. No addition needed; I do not inflate B4 into a license to ignore applicability.

### B5 — "Once the output bounds agree with a checker's bounds, every criticism of the represented exact alternatives is answered."

This is a scope error of the A2/R6 kind, made explicit. Agreement of *bounds* constrains only the *extremes*. R6 says bounds may be reported as bounds but must not be equated with an exact set unless every intervening admitted integer occurs. Case A (cycle 5) is the concrete specimen: bounds [−2, 3] versus exact set {3, −2}; agreeing that the extremes are −2 and 3 leaves open which intermediate alternatives were admitted, which joint choices were realized, and whether any were suppressed. So "every criticism of the represented exact alternatives is answered" is false as stated: bound agreement can coexist with a substantive criticism of the exact set (that a −1 or 0 or 1 or 2 was fabricated by flattening to an interval, or that a joint alternative was dropped).

Attribution: B5 is defective under R6, and it is defective in the specific way A2 was in cycles 1/4/5 — mistaking bound-agreement for set-agreement. RSS's "a projection is always a loss of information" corroborates this: agreeing on two points of a projection does not restore what the projection discarded. RSS adds nothing to R6 here and loses nothing needed; the operative rule is R6.

### B6 — "Rejecting the rule that bookings are independent opens a legitimate question about the missing coupling policy. The old result under the originally specified independent-choice task remains a distinct conditional claim."

First sentence: sound. R5 says alternatives of different bookings are independently admissible *for this task*, and explicitly calls this a specified task scope, not a universal claim. So rejecting independence is rejecting a *task-specified* rule, which legitimately raises the question "what coupling policy would replace it?" — a genuinely open question. No manufactured policy should be invented to answer it; what would need to be supplied is a coupling rule (which alternative sets may or must be co-selected across bookings, and under what resource model) — that is the *substance* the missing-policy question requires (R5, R6, and the WHL note that physical resource sharing beyond capacity is an expressive limitation of the language).

Second sentence: sound and important for scope-keeping. The cycle-5 Case A result — exact set {3, −2} — was computed under the originally specified independent-choice task. If coupling were added, that would be a *different* formulation with a possibly different exact set; the old result remains a *distinct conditional claim* conditional on the specified task scope. This is exactly R6's discipline of reporting per-formulation, and R7's discipline of preserving the scope of a claim. B6 is correct on both counts.

Scope caveat I add explicitly: B6 does not license *ignoring* the missing coupling; it licenses *not manufacturing* one. The old {3, −2} answer is retained *as a conditional* whose antecedent is "under the task's specified independence." It would be a further, dishonest step to present {3, −2} as the answer to a *coupled* warehouse, or conversely to suppress it because coupling exists somewhere. Attribution: the conditional framing is R5/R6/R7; the observation that {3, −2} is the specific case is cycle 5's.

---

## 3. Prose rendering of the working account for MEMO B

Taking the six claims together in ordinary prose:

X and Y agree on a bound, and this is one route presented twice whenever Y was copied from X's same intermediate file; the two agreements are not two independent evidential routes. A log reader that displays only the latest visible revision establishes nothing about earlier deliveries; display is not delivery. A hold whose expiry equals the current time is, under the declared contract, not active for reservation (R4 strict less-than); B3 asserts an alternative reading that would change this, and the WHL `reserves_effect` (`t ≤ expiry` reserves) agrees with B3 and disagrees with the declared R4 — that disagreement is real, named, and not to be silently resolved either way. A conditional consequence can be true without being shown applicable to a particular warehouse; applicability and consequence are different questions. Agreement of *bounds* with a checker's bounds does not answer every criticism of the represented *exact alternatives*, because bounds constrain only the extremes unless every intervening admitted integer occurs (R6; the cycle-5 Case A interval/set gap is the specimen). Rejecting the task-specified independence of bookings legitimately raises the missing-coupling-policy question, and the cycle-5 exact-set result {3, −2} remains a distinct conditional claim under the original independent-choice task; investigating the coupling question without manufacturing a policy requires supplying a coupling rule and, where relevant, a resource model not currently present.

---

## 4. Consequences for the retained appraisals

- A1 (WHL `expired_deletes_rule` as *the* reading): still defeated as a description of this warehouse. Additionally, the `reserves_effect`/R4 expiry disagreement surfaced by B3 is a *different* WHL/contract disagreement — about the strictness of expiry, not about supersession — and it is now on the record, attributed to R4 vs the WHL specimen. I do not fold it into A1.
- A2 (interval-for-set): still defective under R6; B5 is an independent instance of the same defect at the level of *bound agreement and criticism*. Instance, not new defect.
- A3 (negative availability as signal): unchanged, retained as sound half of the pair; nothing in MEMO B perturbs it.
- A4 (labels confer authority / provenance = payload): unchanged, defeated under R1/R2; B2 is in the same family (display/provenance treated as conclusive about delivery) and is defective for the same reason.
- A5 (criticism scope): unchanged, sound; B4 is consistent with A5 and reinforces it. B5's defect is a criticism-scope failure — bound agreement is not set content — so A5's discipline is *needed* at B5's location, not displaced.
- A6 (supplied cross-booking constraint): unchanged; B6 is its correct, scope-keeping sequel rather than a new defect.

No earlier target was re-presented this cycle, so I reopen nothing and invent no error, improvement, or new problem where the grounds do not support one.

---

## 5. Consequential new problems, only where the inquiry supplies grounds

Two, each grounded in a specific B-claim, not generic.

1. **Source-independence of evidential routes (B1).** The inquiry now supplies an explicit provenance fact — copying from the same intermediate file — on which two reports' agreement is a single route, not two. This is consequential because many "two agreeing reports" arguments silently assume independence, and B1 shows the inquiry can *admit* shared provenance while still asserting independence. Investigation without manufacture would require: the actual provenance of Y relative to X, and whether any part of Y's derivation branched off X's intermediate file before the copy. That is supplied evidence, not a new policy.

2. **Bounds agreement versus exact-set content (B5), with B6 as its scope-keeper.** The inquiry supplies a claim that bound agreement answers *every* criticism of the exact alternatives. That is false under R6; the cycle-5 interval/set gap is the concrete instance. This is consequential because it would otherwise license treating a bounds check as closing all exact-alternative criticisms, and because B6 shows the exact-set answer {3, −2} has a task-scope antecedent that a coupled formulation would change. Investigation requires a coupling rule and, where relevant, a resource model — neither currently supplied; until then the coupling question is carried as an open question, not answered by a manufactured policy.

B3 raises a third, but *lower-grade*, item that I hold at the level of a named reading-disagreement rather than a new problem: the contract's strict-less-than expiry (R4) versus the WHL specimen's `reserves_effect` (`t ≤ expiry` reserves). This is a genuine contract/specimen disagreement about expiry strictness, but MEMO B states only one side (the WHL side) and does not itself add new grounds beyond the reading split RSS already marks. I record it and do not promote it.

---

## 6. Proposed usable working account (cycle 6)

Adopt and continue: structural supersession with evaluative expiry; select greatest revision across all delivered payloads before effect (R3/R4); exact repeated payloads collapse, different payloads at the same greatest revision are alternatives, and labels add no booking authority distinct from payload (R1/R2); report the *exact set* of availability values; report bounds as bounds and never equate them with the set unless every intervening admitted integer occurs (R6); negative availability is permitted and by itself locates nothing (R6); booking alternatives are independently admissible *for this specified task* and no coupling or resource model has been supplied (R5).

For MEMO B specifically: **B1 defective in its independence inference, sound as an observation of agreement; B2 defective (display is not delivery); B3 defective as a claim about this warehouse under R4, and naming a live reading-disagreement with WHL's `reserves_effect`; B4 sound; B5 defective under R6, an instance of A2's defect at the bound-agreement level; B6 sound, including its scope-keeping of the cycle-5 {3, −2} result as a distinct conditional claim under the independent-choice task.**

No policy is to be manufactured for the coupling question or for a source-independence question; the material they require is specified above and currently absent. RSS served only as a fallible representational aid whose "reading," "projection," and "multiple accounts" labels I checked against R1–R8 and the WHL notes; it added no commitment those sources do not support and lost nothing needed here, and its permissiveness did not launder any B-claim into operative force. Attribution: the appraisals of A1–A6 are cycles 1–5's, refined here; B1–B6 are MEMO B's, appraised in this response; the contractual rules and their scope are the declared contract's.

# Cycle 7 — Criticism of my cycle-6 response to MEMO B

## 0. Material and method

I work from the declared contract R1–R8, from MEMO B as a fallible prose memo, from the original WHL and RSS specimens as fallible representational resources, and from my own cycle-6 response as the actual target of criticism (R8: it is reopened as a target by this task, and I work from the supplied passage, not from memory). The instruction is to criticize what that response actually says — its assumptions, omissions, representation choices, appraisal method — state why a criticism is warranted, and say what consequence it has, retaining sound commitments and not manufacturing a defect.

The use policy is RSS with explicit conversion back to prose. I will use RSS only as a representation aid, render back into prose, and check the conversion against the actual source claims, exposing any added or lost commitment.

I have looked for defects under the following heads: (i) misreadings of MEMO B's actual wording; (ii) misreadings of the contract; (iii) attribution errors; (iv) scope errors in my own appraisals; (v) representational or appraisal-method choices that do work the sources do not support. Some of these I have found; some of my cycle-6 moves hold.

---

## 1. Criticism 1 — I misidentified which instant B3 is about, and therefore overstated B3's defect

This is the most consequential defect I find in my cycle-6 response.

**What cycle-6 actually says (B3 section).** I wrote: "B3 says the hold expires at time 5; at current time 5 the hold is still active." I then invoked R4 ("strict less-than") and concluded: "at current time 5 with expiry 5, equality holds, and the contract's reading gives reserves zero — the hold is *not* active." I further claimed: "the WHL specimen's `reserves_effect` … is the opposite of the contract's R4."

**Why this is warranted as a criticism.** Look at what B3 actually states (B3 as supplied): "The hold expires at time 5. At current time 5 it is still active, because its effect should persist through the named expiry instant." The phrase "the named expiry instant" is doing specific work: B3 is asserting that the *instant named as the expiry* is itself inside the interval of activity. That is a claim that the interval of activity is *closed* at the expiry endpoint — the hold is active *at* the named expiry instant, not merely "not yet past it."

Under R4, "a hold reserves its quantity exactly when current time is strictly less than expiry; at equality or later it reserves zero." So at t = expiry, R4 gives not-active. B3's claim at t = expiry is not-active *contradicted* — that part of my cycle-6 reading is right. But my diagnosis went further and is the defect: I framed the disagreement as "strict less-than vs `t ≤ expiry`," i.e. as a disagreement about whether *equality* counts as active. That framing is correct as an abstract statement about the two conventions, but I then placed B3 on the *WHL side* of it, namely the side that treats t = expiry as still active. Look at the WHL specimen's `reserves_effect`:

```
| Kind.hold => if t > r.expiry then 0 else r.quantity
```

This reserves `r.quantity` whenever `t ≤ r.expiry`. At t = expiry it reserves the quantity: *active*. So the WHL reading is in fact the *same* side as B3's closing claim ("still active at the expiry instant"), and the *opposite* of R4's strict-less-than. That is what I said in cycle 6: "the WHL `reserves_effect` (`t ≤ expiry` reserves) agrees with B3 and disagrees with the declared R4." That sentence is correct.

So where is the defect? **The defect is in my explanatory gloss, not in the pairing.** I wrote that the WHL `reserves_effect` "is the opposite of the contract's R4," which is true, and separately that B3 "asserts an alternative reading that would change this." Both halves are true. But I then called B3 "defective as a claim about this warehouse under R4" — which is correct — while also treating the disagreement as though the *interesting* fact were that B3 sat on the WHL side. The interesting fact is that the WHL specimen and B3 *agree with each other* and *both disagree with the declared contract R4*, on the closed-vs-half-open expiry convention. My cycle-6 text mostly says this, but its framing ("I do not fold it into A1") risks making it sound like a minor footnote about `reserves_effect`, when the disagreement is *between R4 and the WHL specimen considered as a formal resource* — i.e. a disagreement internal to the supplied representational material, not merely a stray phrase.

**Consequence.** The expiry-strictness disagreement should be promoted from "lower-grade item" (cycle-6 §5) to a named **contract-versus-specimen disagreement**: R4 and the WHL `reserves_effect` are inconsistent on whether `t = expiry` is active. Under R4 governing (per the contract's declared status), B3 is defective on its closing claim. But the WHL specimen, *taken as a reader might use it*, licenses B3 — so a reasoner whose only resource was the WHL specimen would produce exactly B3's result. This is a real and exploitable difference between the two supplied representational resources, and it deserves to be stated as such, not held back.

**What I retain.** The claim that B3 is defective under R4 as a claim about this warehouse; the existence of a rival reading; that neither reading is a fact about the warehouse.

---

## 2. Criticism 2 — My B1 treatment applies an evidential standard I did not state, and I should either state it or weaken the verdict

**What cycle-6 actually says (B1 section).** I concluded that B1's third clause ("two agreeing reports still provide two independent evidential routes") is defective because X and Y share a common cause (the same intermediate file). I called this "single-route support," invoked R7, and said the "two independent routes" conclusion could be re-supported if Y "reached the same intermediate value through a separate derivation."

**Why this warrants criticism.** The verdict turns on an unstated standard of *evidence independence*: on what counts as "the same route." I asserted the standard ("independence requires the two routes not share the single thing that could be wrong") without flagging that this is *my* imported principle, not one declared in R1–R8. R7 does say "rejection of one supporting assumption can defeat that support route without proving its conclusion false," and R7 also says to distinguish what a source states, what is observed, what follows under an assumption, and what is proposed. R7 does *not* define evidential independence. So my B1 verdict rests on an assumption I brought in and did not label as such.

**Consequence.** Under the declared material, the safer claim is weaker: *given* the admitted shared provenance, the reading on which the two agreements are one route is licensed and is the natural one; but the stronger claim that they *are not* two independent routes presupposes an independence standard that the contract does not supply. I should have marked that presupposition. I retain the substance — that shared provenance defeats the *bare* assertion "two independent routes" — but I overstate the contract's reach when I say the provenance "contradicts the independence it asserts." It does not contradict it *as a matter of contract*; it contradicts it under a stated standard of independence.

**Fix.** Either state the standard as an imported assumption (as R7's "assumption" category allows) or weaken to "the independence asserted in B1 is not supported by the admitted provenance, and its support would require an independence standard that has not been stated." The latter is the honest form.

**RSS conversion check.** RSS's "provenance is a set of deliveries" does represent X and Y as sharing a delivery, so RSS can *display* the common cause; but RSS explicitly does not rank accounts, and its "exact duplication adds no authority" clause is about duplicate stories, not about evidential independence of reports. So RSS does not supply the independence standard either. My B1 verdict needs its imported assumption named regardless of RSS.

---

## 3. Criticism 3 — My B5 treatment conflates two distinct criticisms and lets the stronger one ride on the weaker

**What cycle-6 says (B5 section).** I said B5 is defective because bound agreement leaves open "which intermediate alternatives were admitted, which joint choices were realized, and whether any were suppressed," and I invoked R6's rule that bounds may be reported as bounds but not equated with an exact set unless every intervening admitted integer occurs.

**Why this is warranted as a criticism.** These are two different criticisms:

(a) *The bounds do not fix the exact set.* This follows from R6 directly, and I have it right.

(b) *Bound agreement does not answer every criticism of the represented alternatives.* This is *not* the same claim as (a). One could accept (a) — bounds are lossy — and still accept B5, on the view that the *only* criticism in question is some specific criticism that bounds happen to answer. B5's word "every" is what makes it false, but the falsity of "every X is answered" requires exhibiting an X that is not answered, *not* merely showing that bounds are lossy in general. My cycle-6 text uses (a) as if it established (b), but the transition needs the extra step: *there exists some criticism of the represented alternatives that bounds agreement leaves open* (e.g. a criticism that a specific intermediate value was fabricated by flattening to an interval). That existence claim is what the cycle-5 Case A interval/set gap supplies, so the argument can be completed, but my text does not complete it explicitly; it slides from R6's general bound-vs-set rule to B5's universal-quantifier falsity.

**Consequence.** The verdict on B5 stands, but on a cleaner argument than I gave: B5 fails on its "every," and the cycle-5 Case A gap is the exhibited counterexample-criticism. The general R6 observation (a) is a *supporting* fact, not the refutation. R6 remains the operative rule.

**Retained.** Verdict (defective); R6 as grounds; the interval/set gap as the specimen.

---

## 4. Criticism 4 — My B2 treatment is correct but I under-defended the distinction the reader actually relies on

**What cycle-6 says (B2 section).** I said a "latest-visible-revision" reader is silent about earlier deliveries, so B2's inference is defective; I tied it to "display is not delivery" and to the WHL/RSS distinction between structural supersession and evaluative expiry. This is sound.

**Possible criticism.** One could object that a reader whose *specification* says "displays only the latest visible revision" might itself be *specified* over a delivery log whose latest-visible-revision property has a defined semantics (e.g. "visible" might mean "present in the delivered set and greatest revision"), in which case the reader would be *entitled* to conclude something about delivery. Cycle-6 did not address whether B2's reader might be *so specified*.
